analysis.title: Compute Wars!
key_insights: TS Lombard argues AI models are commoditising, so lasting value goes to whoever owns distribution and whoever supplies compute most cheaply. China cannot own Western distribution but can be the low-cost producer of compute, as it was in solar and batteries.

Democrats took both chambers of Congress, with data centres on the ballot. Governors-elect in Texas and Georgia campaigned partly on moratoria. TSL expects slower US permitting and hyperscalers paying for grid upgrades, and says a slower US build reallocates compute demand rather than reducing it.

Nvidia has told data-centre customers worldwide that at least 51% of their services must go to non-Chinese firms. TSL says this narrows the route Chinese labs used to rent Nvidia chips in Southeast Asia and pushes China's biggest buyers onto Huawei, Cambricon and T-Head sooner.

Beijing requires state-funded data centres to use domestic chips, and customs blocked Nvidia's H200 for two months this year. Nvidia's share of China's accelerator shipments fell to 34% in H1 2026, with Huawei at 28%.

On OpenRouter, open-weight models carry 72% of tokens and Chinese labs alone 69%, yet closed models take 73% of spend. TSL reads this as volume moving to the cheap end while spend has not followed yet.
Revolut moved its 2,000 engineers' default coding model from Claude Code and Codex to China's GLM, cutting the bill to about a tenth and keeping frontier models for the hardest work.
H100 rental prices have more than halved since late 2023 and CME lists GPU rental futures, which TSL cites as evidence compute now trades like a commodity.

Node gap: Taiwan has 2nm in volume while China has been stuck at 7nm-class since 2023. TSL argues packaging, interconnect and power matter more as gates approach atomic scale, so lithography is less binding for high-throughput GPUs.

Huawei's CloudMatrix 384 beats Nvidia's GB200 NVL72 by 1.7x on compute and 3.6x on memory, at roughly four times the power. TSL says this is bad economics where power is expensive but not a constraint in China.

Running costs: Inner Mongolia data-centre hubs pay about 4.7 US cents per kWh, around half the US industrial average. China added ten times as much generating capacity as the US last year. On price per TFLOP, Chinese chips now match Nvidia.

A Chinese chip only has to undercut Nvidia's roughly 75% gross margin, not its manufacturing cost. In solar, module prices fell 95% and in batteries pack prices fell 90% as China took more than 80% of manufacturing.

Chinese open models are the default in price-sensitive channels and increasingly built for Chinese chips. DeepSeek V4 launched with day-zero support on Huawei's Ascend, and GLM-5 was reportedly trained on it.

Security: TSL argues privacy concerns about Chinese compute are largely solvable with confidential computing and remote attestation. Alibaba Cloud runs Nvidia GPUs inside Intel TDX enclaves, and Hygon and Huawei have built home-grown equivalents.

Investor implications: not winner-takes-all. Microsoft owns the workflow layer, Amazon much of the development layer and Meta is betting on personal use. TSL expects national owners of distribution, a mix of open and closed models, and compute supplied from China, with risk to the margins of Western hardware names and to Taiwan and Korea.
Macro fallout per TSL: shrinking profits for Western tech and a structurally stronger RMB. TSL says the China Tech Shock is just getting started.

market_movers.rationale: Nvidia's roughly 75% gross margin is the opening for Chinese chips to undercut on price, and its China accelerator share fell to 34% in H1 2026. TSL flags risk to Western hardware margins.
Alibaba Cloud is cited as a leader in confidential compute, running Nvidia GPUs inside Intel TDX enclaves, which supports China's case as a trusted low-cost compute supplier.
TSL says Microsoft owns the workflow layer, which positions it among the owners of distribution.
TSL says Amazon owns much of the development layer.
TSL says Meta is betting on personal use of AI.

sector_views.rationale: Risk falls on the margins of Western hardware names as China becomes the low-cost compute supplier, and on Taiwan and Korea.
TSL expects shrinking profits for Western tech from the China Tech Shock.
TSL notes most Chinese AI baskets rose in the AI sell-off while US peers fell, and expects China to be the low-cost compute producer.

tension_points.bull_case: China can be the cheapest compute supplier: power at about 4.7 US cents per kWh, price per TFLOP matching Nvidia, and a path to undercut Nvidia's ~75% gross margin as it did in solar and batteries.
tension_points.bear_case: China remains at 7nm-class against Taiwan's 2nm, its headline breakthroughs rarely materialise, and Huawei's system uses roughly four times the power. Privacy and trust concerns remain a barrier.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Confidential computing and remote attestation failing to address Western trust concerns, or power costs mattering as in the West, would limit China's reach in Western markets.

theme_stances.key_argument: China cannot own Western distribution but can be the low-cost producer of compute, as it was for solar and batteries.
theme_stances.evidence: China can't own Western distribution, but can be compute's low-cost producer

theme_stances.key_argument: Open-weight models match the frontier within months, so distribution and cheap compute hold the lasting value.
theme_stances.evidence: It's pretty much consensus that models are inherently un-moatable.
